chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a group of people who arrived in Medina and feared the severity of the cold and the length of the days, meaning the state of Ihram from Al-Shajara. They wanted to take from there to Dhat 'Irq so that they could enter Ihram from it. He said, 'No,' while he was angry, 'Whoever enters Medina, he is not permitted to enter Ihram except from Medina.' And whoever forgets the Ihram from the Miqat, let him return to it and enter Ihram from it if there is a time for it; and if there is no time for it, let him proceed and enter Ihram from the place to which he arrived.

key_terms.الشَّجَرَة: Al-Shajara, a specific Miqat near Medina
key_terms.الْإِحْرَام: Ihram, the sacred state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.الْمَدِينَة: Medina, the city and its designated Miqat for pilgrims
key_terms.الْمِيقَات: Miqat, the designated stations or places for entering Ihram
key_terms.ذَات عِرْق: Dhat 'Irq, a specific Miqat located south of Medina
key_terms.وَقْت: Time, referring to the period of Hajj days

ai.seo_question: Where must a pilgrim enter Ihram if they arrive in Medina?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) explicitly rules that Medina serves as the exclusive Miqat for its residents and visitors, rejecting the use of Dhat 'Irq to emphasize the sanctity of the city's boundary. The hadith provides a practical legal distinction for those who miss the Miqat: they must return if time allows, but if the Hajj season has passed, they proceed from their current location, illustrating the Shia principle of ease in ritual obligations.
